Comensals · Field Build · Barcelona

Barcelona Urban Compost

A sensor inside a compost pile, giving decay a voice.

Built from foraged pallets and an off-grid sensor · Work in progress · Full build on Hackster ↗

This started from a simple refusal.. the belief that soil is dirt, death is waste, and decomposition is failure. A compost pile is none of those things, it's a living system running its own world on its own time, and I wanted to build something that could let me understand that, and then set the pile's interior against the city around it.

01 · The Vessel

Foraging the bin

The bin is a cube built entirely from discarded pallets, cut down with a Japanese handsaw and a jigsaw and then reassembled into an open crate. Pallet wood is the packaging the city forgets, and now that I had started searching for it I can't unsee it.. it's everywhere if you look. The gaps between the slats aren't necessarily a flaw either, because compost needs to breathe and drain anyway.

Nothing in the infrastructure is a new material, which felt like the only honest way to build a project about waste...

02 · The Layering

Layering the trouble

Compost really just wants two things in conversation with each other.. greens, which are the wet nitrogen things like peels and coffee grounds and the orange rinds people leave at a table, and browns, which are the dry carbon things like cardboard and dead leaves and shredded paper. You keep it roughly even with the browns slightly winning, damp like a wrung-out sponge, and you turn it whenever you remember to.

You're not really managing waste so much as hosting a relationship.. the bacteria and the fungi and the worms that find their way in are the ones doing the work, on a timeline that isn't yours, and mostly your job is just to not get in the way.

03 · The Nervous System

Giving it a nervous system

The electronics are what let the pile report its own interior:

  • Barduino 4.0.2 (IAAC's ESP32-S3 board) for the microcontroller and the wifi
  • Adafruit Seesaw I2C soil sensor, which reads temperature and capacitance (a moisture proxy, since water changes how the soil holds a charge) from one probe
  • DFRobot Solar Power Manager 5V + LiPo battery + USB Li-Ion charger, so the bin can power itself off-grid.. which felt like the only honest way to power something that lives outdoors
  • Google Sheets + Google Apps Script as the logbook, written over wifi, with each reading landing next to Barcelona's outdoor air temperature pulled in automatically from an open weather API

The capacitive sensor matters here because, unlike a cheap resistive probe, it doesn't corrode sitting in wet compost, so it actually survives living there. The sketch itself is small.. the Seesaw library does most of the work, reading the temperature and the capacitance every 60 seconds and printing them to serial, and from there the Barduino pushes it all up to the sheet.

// soil sensor.. reads temp + capacitance every 60s

#include "Adafruit_seesaw.h"
Adafruit_seesaw ss;

void setup() {
  Serial.begin(115200);
  if (!ss.begin(0x36)) {
    Serial.println("ERROR! seesaw not found");
    while(1) delay(1);
  }
}

void loop() {
  float tempC = ss.getTemp();
  uint16_t capread = ss.touchRead(0);
  Serial.print("Temperature: "); Serial.println(tempC);
  Serial.print("Capacitive: ");  Serial.println(capread);
  delay(60000);
}

What I was really after was two lines.. the heat of the decay, and the air of the city. The idea, or the hope, was that the compost would hold its own warmth, sitting steadier and higher and smoothing out the daily spikes that the open air can't really escape.

What broke (the real documentation)

I soldered the sensor input on backwards and had to desolder it and redo the whole thing, which was a productive kind of failure because it forced me to actually understand the wiring instead of just copying a diagram.

And before I automated anything, I was copying numbers out of the serial monitor into the spreadsheet by hand.. the dumbest possible version of the pipeline, but it did prove the data was there before I trusted the code.

Getting live data into Sheets meant fighting a Google Apps Script that emailed me a "summary of failures" every single day.. and it honestly keeps doing it to this day.

AI (Claude) was a tool in the process too, mostly for debugging the script and helping me think through the narrative.

04 · The Return

What it's really for

The thing is, the compost doesn't actually need the sensor.. it composted for millions of years before the Barduino ever existed. The instrument isn't really for the pile, it's for me.. a kind of translation device sitting between two temporalities, mine and the soil's, a way to slow myself down enough to perceive a process I'm structurally just too fast to notice.

This is a work in progress, and that's sort of the point.. the loop of scraps to soil to the next batch takes longer than any deadline, so it was always going to be difficult to see immediate results. The compost pile isn't really a metaphor for community.. it's closer to the instructions for one.

Rot is always better with company.

This knowledge has no owner.
